label: Parenting Adult Children
framing: There comes a day when the parent must stop steering and start blessing, when the open hand replaces the firm grip. Scripture honors the long love of a parent while it also makes room for the child to leave, to cleave, to become a person before God in their own right.
cultural: In the ancient household the father's authority ran long and deep, and yet even there the Scripture said a man shall leave his father and mother, a quiet revolution that set the grown child loose to form a new household. The Bible knows the ache of release, naming it again and again in parents who must let their children walk into lives they cannot control.
historical: Eli, the priest around 1100 BC, learned too late that influence over grown sons is not the same as control, while Monica, the mother of Augustine in the fourth century, prayed for her wayward son across decades and lived to see him turn. The church has long counseled parents of adult children toward prayer and presence rather than pressure, the slow patience of a God who waits.
application: Move from manager to consultant, offering counsel when asked and holding your tongue when it is not. Respect the household they have formed, especially the spouse, and do not make your child choose between you. Pray more than you advise. And keep the relationship warm even through disagreement, since the open door matters more than winning the point.

verses.text: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.
verses.where: At the first marriage the narrator draws a lasting conclusion: a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife. The note says this answers the not good of being alone in every generation. Leaving home is not a failure of the family God made; it is written into it from the start.

verses.text: His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”
verses.where: At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, and Mary tells her grown son. The site's note says she states the need and leaves the response to him, and when he answers that his hour has not yet come, she tells the servants to do whatever he says. A mother brings a concern to her adult son and then lets him act in his own way.

verses.text: Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home. May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me. May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” And she kissed them as they wept aloud and said, “Surely we will return with you to your people.”
verses.where: Naomi, widowed and bereaved of both sons, tells her two daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' homes, and she blesses them with the LORD's kindness and rest. She does not hold them by need, though she needs them badly. One goes and one stays, and Naomi's blessing covers both choices.

verses.text: Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.
verses.where: Rebekah overhears Isaac and tells her grown son Jacob to do exactly as she says. The note points out that she plans every step and Jacob's part is to obey. The deception that follows splits the family for twenty years. Scripture records a parent running an adult child's life, and what it cost.

verses.text: But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice.
verses.where: Samuel, a faithful prophet raised in God's house, appoints his sons as judges in his old age, and they take bribes and pervert justice. The Bible does not explain it or blame him for it. A godly parent can have grown children who do not walk in his ways.

verses.text: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
verses.where: The elder writes to his friend Gaius that he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth. He means his children in the faith, and the joy is a parent's joy. It comes by hearing, at a distance, of a life lived well that he no longer directs.

verses.text: The father of a righteous man will greatly rejoice, and he who fathers a wise son will delight in him. May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice!
verses.where: The father of a righteous son rejoices, and the son is told to let his father and mother be glad. The same passage asks the grown child not to despise a mother when she is old. Honor and delight run in both directions between parents and grown children.

verses.text: Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father.
verses.where: Grandchildren are the crown of the old, and a father is the glory of his children. The proverb sees a family across three generations. A parent's role does not end when children leave; it changes shape, and often becomes a crown.

verses.text: Then he blessed Joseph and said: “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all harm— may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.”
verses.where: Old and ill, Jacob blesses Joseph by blessing Joseph's sons, naming the God who had been his shepherd all his life. The note says he crosses his hands and puts his right hand on the younger, and Genesis shows again that God's blessing is a gift, not a right of rank. The last work of a parent in Genesis is often a blessing spoken over grown children and grandchildren.

verses.text: ‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.’
verses.where: God gives Aaron the words to speak over Israel: the LORD bless you and keep you, make his face shine on you, and give you peace. So the priests put God's name on his people. Many parents have spoken these words over grown children, asking for them what a parent can no longer give.

misread.taken: Honor your father and mother is sometimes used by parents to claim a say over an adult child's marriage, work, money or faith, as if the commandment meant obedience for life and disagreement were dishonor.
misread.says: The commandment is given to the whole people, adults included, and Scripture shows what honor means: respect, gratitude and care, including practical support in old age, as the site's notes on 1 Timothy 5 and Mark 7 point out. The obedience Paul asks of children in Ephesians 6 is asked of children in the home, and in the Lord. Genesis 2 says a grown son leaves his father and mother. An adult child can honor a parent and still make his own choices before God; the commandment asks for honor, not control.
misread.text: Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.

whole: There is no ceremony for the day a parent stops steering. It happens in pieces: a decision you were not asked about, a holiday spent with the other family, a career or a city or a spouse you would not have chosen. For many parents the hardest part is not the distance but the silence about faith, a grown child who no longer prays or goes to church, or who believes differently. Others carry the opposite weight, a grown child who cannot leave, or who comes back in crisis. And many parents are quietly grieving the end of the years when they were needed every day.

Scripture expects the change. From the second chapter of Genesis a son leaves his father and mother, and the Bible shows what happens when parents will not let go: Rebekah ran her grown son's life and split her family for twenty years. It is also honest that faithful parents can raise children who go another way. Samuel's sons took bribes, and the text does not blame Samuel or explain it. Most of the pain in this season comes from a love that has not yet changed its form, and from a fear, which most of us share, that if we are not in control, no one is.

So the Bible's wisdom is to move from steering to blessing. Mary at Cana is a quiet model: she named the need to her grown son and then stepped back and told others to do what he said. Naomi blessed her daughters-in-law to go and meant it. Offer counsel when it is asked for and sometimes once when it is not, then leave it. Keep the door open, the table set and the phone answered, without making love conditional on agreement. Honor your grown child's marriage, which comes before you now. Help with money or a place to stay in ways that strengthen them rather than keep them dependent, and say no when a yes would harm them. And pray, which is the one form of influence that does not shrink as they grow.

Underneath it is a trust that each child belongs first to God. The elder's greatest joy was to hear that his children walked in the truth, and he heard it from far away. Jacob's last act was to bless, naming the God who had shepherded him all his life. A parent of grown children can still do that: speak the old blessing over them, the LORD bless you and keep you, and trust the God who keeps them when they are out of sight. The love does not end. It becomes an open hand.
deep.sit: What would it sound like to bless your grown child this month, in words or in a choice, without attaching advice to it?

prayer.lead: The end of a psalm about a household, asking to see your children's children and peace on God's people.
prayer.text: May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life, that you may see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel!
